newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban fight Shi'ites in conquered city.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban fight Shi'ites in conquered city.

text.p: Heavy fighting erupted in this northern Afghan city on Tuesday after armed Shi'ite Moslem residents killed three looters said to belong to the purist Islamic Taleban militia, witnesses said.
Machinegun fire rattled through the streets amid the crash of rocket-propelled grenades as Taleban fighters battled Shi'ite Moslems in the city's northern district of Saidabad.
The fighting started late in the afternoon and continued into the night, when tracer bullets could be seen flying around.
It was not immediately clear if the troops loyal to ethnic Uzbek general Abdul Malik, who allied with the Taleban last week, were involved in the clashes that flared in many parts of the city.
Tension rose after armed men in the mainly Shi'ite Saidabad district shot dead three suspected Taleban looters.
One witness said one of Malik's generals had dissuaded the Taleban forces from entering Saidabad soon after the killings, but shooting and explosions were heard a few hours later.
The Taleban and Malik's men are supposed to be operating as a joint security force in the north, but it was not immediately clear if both groups were in action against the Shi'ites.
"All the people started fighting the Taleban because they were taking television sets and everything from people's homes, even children's toys," said Sadiqullah, a Shi'ite resident.
"They are not human. If they were human we would join them, but they are wild men," he said, quivering with anger.
Saidabad is a stronghold of the anti-Taleban Hezb-i-Wahdat Shi'ite militiamen when the city was controlled by opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Many Shi'ite fighters are said to have fled to nearby mountains.
Hundreds of Taleban fighters arrived in Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday, apparently to help disarm opposition factions.
"They brought in 500 to 600 Tleban, some by road, some by air," Brigadier General Abdul Jamil told reporters at the joint civil and miliatry airport outside Mazar-i-Sharif.
"Many Taleban will arrive here," he said. "We will disarm everyone opposed to the Islamic state and Islamic Sharia law."
Among the Taleban arrivals was Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, who held talks with Malik and his Taleban military corps commander Mullah Abdul Razzaq.
He told a news conference that the talks had focused on a mixed Taleban-Malik security council and "commanders who previously made problems for the people of this area".
He said Taleban recognised that Malik had enough forces to control security, but also said that Uzbek general had asked Taleban to send 3,000 Taleban fighters to the north.
"The security situation in Mazar-i-Sharif is good, but we hope to improve it in the future," he said.

Asked about concerns expressed by Russia about Taleban's latest territorial gains, Ghous said: "Our policy is to have good relations with all countries, espacially our neighbours. We don't want others to make problems for us."
He urged his neighbours to take the example of Pakistan and Saudi Arabia and recognise the Taleban government in Kabul, saying such recognition was "our right and not our hope".
Schools, colleges and many shops remained closed in Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday, reflecting an uneasy relationship between the mainly ethnic Pasthun Taleban and Malik's troops.
"Trouble is not over yet," said a foreign resident, who asked not be named. "People were smiling when Malik's troops arrived, but now they fear the Taleban would disarm them."
